items.note: The Mālava king is called Harsha in the Udaipur prasasti and Siyaka in the Pānāhedā inscription; editor takes this as proof that the two are identical.
Arthūnā inscription gives the Vasishtha sacrificial-pit myth of the Paramāras' creation; editor calls it a later invention to glorify the family.
Imposts on goods sold in the bazaar (sugar, cotton, coconuts, salt, butter, oil, cloth) listed in the Arthūnā inscription; a Paramāra-branch parallel for trade and market levies.
Monthly and festival levies on traders' houses, braziers' shops, distillers and a gambling house in the town, collected on the fourteenth of each bright half.
Includes a hāraka of barley on a water-wheel among the taxes.
